prize_parts.citation: For a visionary, densely patterned prose oeuvre that turns memory, the body and dream into an expansive metaphysical architecture, with a poet's attention to the sentence.

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: Cărtărescu alone, in one prize part. The chair's question about extension versus restatement is the right test, and I can only answer it from public knowledge. As publicly described, the Orbitor trilogy (Blinding) builds its world from the body, childhood in Bucharest and a dream-logic cosmology. Solenoid is described as taking a different form: a more diaristic, first-person, essayistic frame around a narrator's obsessions, with the metaphysical speculation made explicit. If that description holds, the later book changes the structure and the narrating stance and does not simply repeat the earlier imagery. That is evidence of renewal in method, not of equal quality, and I cannot verify it by reading. Under the committee's criteria, the voice is distinctive and the formal ambition is sustained over decades. The imaginative and intellectual range is wide, and the work is a body of work, not a single successful book. I have narrowed the citation in one respect. Palm is right that coverage of the poetry in translation is thin, so the claim rests on the prose. I have therefore dropped the word 'encyclopedic' and kept the poet's attention to the sentence as a qualified phrase. If the committee cannot confirm the poetic dimension, that phrase should come out and the citation should stand on the prose.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation remains dependence on translation for very long, dense, musical prose, together with the unresolved risk of self-repetition across large volumes. If the later books turn out to restate the earlier cycle, my claim of sustained quality over the whole oeuvre weakens materially. My coverage of the early fiction and the poetry is uneven, so the full corpus may be mis-weighted in either direction. I also take Mattson's and Sem-Sandberg's objection to my round-1 asymmetry: I cannot treat translation loss as a discount for Michon's French while treating Cărtărescu's Romanian as safer. I no longer rest anything on that comparison. What remains of my difference with the Michon case is only the breadth question under the whole-oeuvre criterion, and that is a judgment, not a finding.

responses.point: Palm ranks Cărtărescu first and reads the late large works as enlarging the world of the earlier ones. She proposes a test: name what changes between Blinding and Solenoid. She admits that coverage of his poetry in translation is thin, so the prose carries most of the case.
responses.response: I accept her test and her admission, and I have adjusted my citation accordingly. My answer to the test is the one in my case: from public descriptions, Solenoid changes the narrating frame and structure relative to the Orbitor cycle. I hold that as a reasoned expectation, not a verified reading. I agree that the poetry should not be counted toward the claim unless the committee can see it in translation. We also share a limit that I should state plainly. Both of us have placed him first partly on a sense of scale that translation may flatter, so the committee should test it on the sentences and not on the size of the books.

responses.point: Mattson ranks Michon first and asks me, in effect, why translation risk should count against compressed French prose and not against dense Romanian prose. She also says the committee should confirm that his later books keep the standard of Small Lives and The Eleven.
responses.response: The challenge is fair and I withdraw the implied asymmetry. Translation loss is a shared condition of this list, and it does not separate Cărtărescu from Michon. My remaining hesitation about Michon is narrower: with a deliberately small corpus, I find it harder to judge from public knowledge whether the project is renewed across books or perfected in a few. You raise the same uncertainty about his later work, and I think that is the right thing for the committee to test. I would not treat it as a flaw in the writing. It may reflect a limit in what I know. I also share your caution about Cărtărescu's very long forms, which is why my preference rests on whether the structure changes between books.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg ranks Michon first. He asks me which of Cărtărescu's late books extend the cycle rather than restate it, and he argues that the compact oeuvre shows sustained quality through consistency, though significance is the harder criterion.
responses.response: I have answered the first part above and have said how little I can verify it. On his distinction I agree that consistency in a compact oeuvre is a real form of sustained quality, and I accept that it is not a lesser form. Where I still differ is on significance across the body of work: a wider range of forms gives the committee more evidence to judge it from, but it does not guarantee that the significance is greater. I would put it this way. The criteria do not settle the difference, and the committee's judgment on Cărtărescu versus Michon turns on that point, not on the size of the corpus.

responses.point: Olsson ranks Adonis first for a decades-long reworking of Arabic poetic language through myth, fragmentation and argument with the tradition. He asks whether evidence from the poems themselves, kept separate from reception and from the essays, supports a claim of the highest formal and linguistic achievement.
responses.response: I cannot supply passage-level evidence from the Arabic, and I should be candid that my third-place ranking rests partly on reception and on uneven translations. That is why he is my second alternative and not my first choice. I agree with his own caution that a reputation for influence is not evidence of quality. I also agree that the critical work belongs to the same project. I would add that an assessment of the later volumes against the early landmarks needs expert reports on the originals, which the committee does not yet have. Without them I cannot put Adonis above a candidate whose formal departure I can examine in translation, though I do not regard that as a verdict against him.

responses.point: Carlberg ranks Wright first for novels that rebuild narrative form from a living Indigenous oral tradition. She names Cărtărescu as her first alternative, and she thinks the choice between them turns on which formal departure is more convincing.
responses.response: I agree that this is where the real difference lies, and I agree with her that it cannot be resolved by assertion. Her point that Wright's departure draws on a living oral tradition, not a private cosmology, is a strong argument about significance, and it is why Wright remains my first alternative. My preference for Cărtărescu rests on the longer record from which sustained quality can be judged. Her own concession about thin knowledge of Wright's later work shows that the uncertainty is real on both sides. I would not claim that either position has the edge on the evidence we hold.

uncertainties: I have not independently verified any text. My account of the difference between Blinding and Solenoid comes from public descriptions, not from a comparison of the volumes.
How much of the density and musicality of Cărtărescu's Romanian survives translation, and whether the available translations are representative of the originals.
Coverage of Cărtărescu's poetry and early fiction in translation is thin, so the claim of achievement across genres rests largely on the prose.
Whether the later large books extend the earlier cycle or repeat its motifs remains open. If they repeat it, my case for sustained quality weakens.
How to weigh a compact oeuvre such as Michon's against a long one under the whole-oeuvre criterion is an unresolved judgment, and my knowledge of the later books by Michon and Wright is thin.
My assessment of Adonis rests on reception and uneven translations, and expert reading of the Arabic originals would be needed to test it.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile, which records no connection to any shortlisted writer. I share Academy and committee membership, and my 2019 election round, with other members, and that is not a connection to any candidate. My practice as a novelist is context only and is not evidence for or against any candidate. This note is updated only to confirm that nothing in round 2 changes it.
